intro.es: A cartographer helps restore old place names to a town map and discovers that preservation still requires a choice about whose memory becomes official.
intro.en: A cartographer helps restore old place names to a town map and discovers that preservation still requires a choice about whose memory becomes official.

mission.es: Consider how a map can preserve local history while also narrowing the range of histories it represents.
mission.en: Consider how a map can preserve local history while also narrowing the range of histories it represents.

content.targetText:
The council invited me to help restore older place names to its digital map. The proposal followed a familiar complaint: new street signs honoured developers and distant benefactors, while names used by residents for generations survived only in conversation. I liked the purpose of the project. I had spent my childhood hearing my grandmother call the eastern footbridge the Washer's Crossing, although the sign beside it said New Mill Link. When I opened the archive, I expected to find the old names waiting there like misplaced keys. Instead I found competing spellings, uncertain boundaries and explanations that contradicted one another. The archive held three versions of the crossing's name. One referred to laundry carried to the river; another to a woman called Washburn who had once rented nearby rooms; the third seemed to have been invented by a journalist who thought the first version sounded picturesque. A map could show only a short label at that scale. Choosing one would make the others harder to find.

At our first meeting, the heritage committee wanted the name that appeared most often in its records. That seemed an impartial rule until we asked why some accounts had been recorded and others had not. The town's early clerks wrote down what property owners called a place. People who rented rooms, crossed the river to work or used the bank for washing appeared in the records mainly when someone else complained about them. Their words had not been counted with the same care as their presence. A frequency test would therefore reproduce the archive's uneven attention while presenting the result as a neutral fact. I suggested we invite residents to contribute names and stories. The committee agreed, but its invitation still went through the council website and a paper notice in the library. The people most likely to answer were already practised at making themselves legible to official institutions. Our broader consultation might diversify the record without escaping its old gatekeepers.

One response complicated the crossing further. A retired nurse sent a photograph of a faded sign reading Mercy Steps, taken before the footbridge had been rebuilt. She wrote that patients had once crossed there on their way to the small hospital. Another resident disputed her account: the sign, he said, had belonged to a path thirty metres downstream, and the photograph's angle concealed the difference. Both accounts were plausible. The nurse had kept an object; the other resident remembered the geography. The committee asked me to mark the sign's location as uncertain and keep the two stories in a note. The digital map could accommodate that uncertainty in a panel opened by a click. The sign installed on the street could not. We were designing two maps at once: one that admitted ambiguity, and another whose authority depended on appearing to have resolved it.

I visited my grandmother before we chose the label. She laughed when I asked about the washer, because she had always thought the name referred to the river's rough sound after rain, not to people cleaning clothes. She could offer no source beyond the fact that her mother had said it that way. I wanted to treat her account with deference, partly because I loved her and partly because I had made her crossing the emblem of our project. But affection could not settle the word's origin, any more than a clerk's handwriting could. She asked me why the map had to decide. People, she said, had managed to cross the bridge while calling it different things. I answered that emergency services, visitors and delivery drivers needed a stable reference. She agreed, then asked whether stability required pretending that the reference was the whole story. I had no easy answer. A label helps people find a place; it can also teach them which past they are expected to find there.

We eventually printed Washer's Crossing on the new sign, with a small mark directing readers to the digital note. The note described the alternate names and the limits of our evidence. It did not give each account equal space: the committee insisted on a principal story, and I wrote it. At the unveiling, a councillor said we had returned the bridge to its true identity. I did not correct him in front of the cameras. Later I wondered whether my silence had made the note's careful qualifications irrelevant. A passer-by might see the sign every day and never open the note. Yet removing the sign would have left the old developer's name in place, carrying its own unexamined claim to permanence. The project had preserved something real, though it could not preserve every relation people had with the river. I now think the most honest map is not one without choices. It is one that makes its choices traceable, so that a name beneath the name remains possible to recover.
